what: Corteva sells seeds and crop chemicals to farmers. Its seed business develops and licenses corn, soybean and other crop varieties with engineered traits for yield, drought tolerance and insect resistance; its crop protection business sells herbicides, insecticides and fungicides.
customers: Farmers worldwide, reached through agricultural retailers and distributors, with the largest markets in North America and Brazil.
money: Corn, soybean and other crop seed, plus trait licensing to other seed companies.
Herbicides, insecticides, fungicides and biological crop inputs.
moat: Developing a seed trait takes a decade and hundreds of millions of dollars in research and regulatory approval, and the resulting intellectual property is protected and licensed to competitors. Farmers also buy the seed that produced the best yield on their own land, which makes switching risky for them and the incumbent position durable.
risks: Free cash flow was about negative $149.0M, because agricultural working capital swings enormously with the planting season and crop prices.
Revenue has been flat at $16.9B to $17.5B for four years, as crop prices fell and farmers economised on inputs.
Farmer income determines everything here, and it has been squeezed by lower crop prices against high input costs.
Generic competition in crop protection has intensified, particularly from Chinese manufacturers, which pressures prices on off-patent chemistry.
Sixteen analysts average a $13.03 target against an $8.12 price, a 60% gap that reflects very different views on the farm economy.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 7.1 times earnings, 1.9 times EV/EBITDA and 0.31 times sales — strikingly low multiples.
Cash of $4.5B against $2.9B of debt is a net cash position, which is unusual for a company of this size.
Seed trait intellectual property takes a decade to develop and is licensed to competitors, generating royalty income.
Farmers must plant every year regardless of the economy, which makes demand far steadier than for most industrial inputs.
The world needs more food from the same amount of land, which is the long-term driver of seed technology demand.
watch: Seed pricing and volumes separately from crop protection. The seed business has intellectual property protection and the crop protection business increasingly does not, and they deserve different multiples.
view: Corteva is two businesses with very different competitive positions sharing a share price, and the market appears to be valuing the whole thing on the weaker half. The seed business develops traits — drought tolerance, insect resistance, yield — that take a decade and enormous research spending to create, are patent-protected, and get licensed to competitors who pay royalties. That is a genuine intellectual property business with real pricing power, and farmers compound it by buying whatever produced the best yield on their own fields.

The crop protection business is weaker and getting weaker. As chemistry comes off patent, Chinese generic manufacturers enter and price falls. That is a structural erosion, not a cycle, and it applies to an increasing share of the portfolio over time. Corteva is responding with new chemistry and biologicals, which is the right response and an expensive one.

On top of that sits the farm economy, which has been poor. Crop prices fell while input costs stayed high, so farmer income was squeezed and farmers economised — buying cheaper seed, skipping a fungicide pass, delaying purchases. Revenue has been flat at about $17 billion for four years as a result. The negative free cash flow of $149 million is mostly agricultural working capital, which swings violently with the planting season, rather than anything operational.

At 7.1 times earnings, 1.9 times EV/EBITDA and 0.31 times sales, with $4.5 billion of cash against $2.9 billion of debt, this is priced as though the farm downturn were permanent. It is not — farmers plant every year, and a bad farm economy is one of the more reliably cyclical things in the world. The sixteen analysts at $13.03 against $8.12 are modelling a recovery. What I would want to know before agreeing is the seed business’s pricing and volumes on their own, because that is the half worth owning, and the consolidated figures let the weaker half obscure it.
bull: The farm economy recovers, seed trait intellectual property keeps earning royalties and pricing power, and 1.9 times EV/EBITDA on a net-cash balance sheet rerates substantially.
bear: Crop prices stay low and farmers keep economising, Chinese generics erode crop protection pricing permanently, and flat revenue persists for years.
